discovery.note: The first element found by spectroscopy, from two blue lines in mineral water.

radioactive.note: A major fallout product of Chernobyl and Fukushima.

elementalForm.description: Caesium's single 6s electron is very far from the nucleus and easily shared; the metallic bonding is so weak that caesium melts at 28.5 °C.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
appearance: Soft, pale-gold metal that melts on a warm day.
summary: Caesium is the most reactive stable metal. The second is defined by the vibrations of caesium-133 atoms: exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles.
uses: Atomic clocks that define the second
facts: Caesium, gold and copper are the only metals that are clearly colored rather than grey or silvery.
hazards: Explodes on contact with water; Cs-137 is a radiation hazard.

discovery.note: Isolated by electrolysis; Carl Scheele had recognized barium oxide in 1772.

nameOrigin: Greek barys, heavy, for the dense mineral barite.

elementalForm.description: Barium shares two 6s electrons per atom in a soft metallic lattice.

originNote: Made mostly by slow neutron capture in aging stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal that quickly oxidizes.
summary: Barium is a heavy alkaline-earth metal. Barium sulfate is so insoluble that patients can swallow it safely for X-ray imaging, even though soluble barium salts are poisonous.
uses: Barium sulfate for X-ray imaging and drilling mud
facts: Barium sulfate blocks X-rays, outlining the gut on medical images.

elementalForm.description: Lanthanum contributes three valence electrons (5d1 6s2) to metallic bonding, the pattern shared by most lanthanides.

bulk.note: Real stacking is ABAC (double hcp); drawn as simple hcp.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Soft, silvery-white metal that tarnishes in air.
summary: Lanthanum gives the lanthanide series its name. A hybrid car battery can contain several kilograms of lanthanum.
facts: Lanthanum-nickel alloy can soak up hydrogen like a sponge.

discovery.by: Jöns Jacob Berzelius; Wilhelm Hisinger; Martin Klaproth
discovery.note: Found as an oxide in the mineral cerite.

nameOrigin: The dwarf planet Ceres, discovered in 1801.

elementalForm.description: Cerium's single 4f electron can join the metallic bonding, which lets cerium switch between valences and gives it unusual phase changes.

allotropes.name: Gamma cerium
allotropes.note: Face-centered cubic, stable at room temperature.

allotropes.name: Alpha cerium
allotropes.note: A denser fcc form under pressure or cold.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
summary: Cerium is the most abundant rare-earth element, more common in the crust than copper. Scraped cerium-iron alloy throws sparks, which is how lighter flints work.
facts: Despite being a 'rare earth', cerium is about as abundant as copper.
hazards: Metal can ignite when scratched; low toxicity.

nameOrigin: Greek prasios didymos, green twin, for its green salts.

elementalForm.description: Praseodymium shares three valence electrons; its 4f electrons stay mostly local and give magnetic properties.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal that develops a green oxide coat.
summary: Praseodymium is a rare-earth metal used in strong magnets and in yellow-green glass and ceramic colors.
facts: Praseodymium-doped glass slows light dramatically in research experiments.

elementalForm.description: Neodymium shares three valence electrons; its four unpaired 4f electrons stay on each atom and give strong magnetism in compounds.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Neodymium makes the strongest permanent magnets known, Nd2Fe14B, found in headphones, wind turbines and electric cars.
facts: A neodymium magnet can lift over 1,000 times its own weight.
hazards: Low toxicity; magnets can pinch skin badly.

discovery.by: Jacob Marinsky; Lawrence Glendenin; Charles Coryell
discovery.note: Identified among uranium fission products at Oak Ridge.

nameOrigin: Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods.

radioactive.note: Used in luminous paint and nuclear batteries.

elementalForm.description: Promethium metal shares three valence electrons like its lanthanide neighbors.

originNote: No stable isotopes; only about half a kilogram exists in Earth's crust at any time, from uranium fission. It is made in reactors.
appearance: Silvery metal; its salts glow pale blue or green from their own radioactivity.
summary: Promethium is the only lanthanide with no stable isotopes. It was finally found among the fission products of the Manhattan Project.
uses: Nuclear batteries for pacemakers and space probes (historically)
facts: In 2024 chemists at Oak Ridge characterized a promethium complex in solution for the first time, almost 80 years after its discovery.

nameOrigin: The mineral samarskite, named after Russian mining officer Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets: the first element named (indirectly) after a person.

radioactive.note: 14.99% of natural samarium; used in samarium-neodymium dating.
13.82%; observationally stable, a strong neutron absorber.

elementalForm.description: Samarium shares three valence electrons in a metallic lattice with an unusual nine-layer stacking.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
appearance: Silvery metal, fairly stable in air.
summary: Samarium-cobalt magnets keep their strength at high temperatures, making them ideal for aerospace and military motors.
facts: Samarium was the first element named after a person, via the mineral samarskite.

elementalForm.description: Europium keeps a half-filled 4f7 shell and shares only two 6s electrons, so it behaves like barium: soft, low-density and very reactive.

originNote: Made almost entirely by rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Silvery metal that oxidizes rapidly in air.
summary: Europium is the most reactive lanthanide. Its glowing compounds made the red of color TV screens and are hidden in euro banknotes as an anti-forgery mark.
uses: Red and blue phosphors in screens and LED lamps
facts: Euro banknotes glow under UV light thanks to europium compounds.

discovery.note: Detected spectroscopically; isolated by Lecoq de Boisbaudran in 1886.

nameOrigin: The mineral gadolinite, named after Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin.

elementalForm.description: Gadolinium (4f7 5d1 6s2) shares three valence electrons; its seven unpaired 4f electrons make it ferromagnetic just below room temperature.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Gadolinium has seven unpaired electrons, which makes its compounds excellent MRI contrast agents. It is ferromagnetic only below 20 °C.
facts: Gadolinium-157 absorbs neutrons better than any other stable isotope.
biology: None; free gadolinium ions are toxic, so MRI agents lock them in cages.
hazards: Free ions are toxic; metal is low hazard.

elementalForm.description: Terbium shares three valence electrons; its 4f electrons give strong magnetism.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Terbium compounds glow bright green and its alloy Terfenol-D changes shape in a magnetic field more than any other material.
uses: Green phosphors in lamps and screens
facts: Terfenol-D stretches noticeably when magnetized, turning magnetic signals into sound.

discovery.note: Took over 30 attempts to separate from holmium oxide.

elementalForm.description: Dysprosium shares three valence electrons; its many unpaired 4f electrons give one of the largest magnetic moments of any element.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
summary: A few percent of dysprosium keeps neodymium magnets working at the high temperatures in electric-car motors and wind turbines.
facts: Its name means 'hard to get' because separating it was so difficult.

discovery.by: Marc Delafontaine; Jacques-Louis Soret; Per Teodor Cleve
discovery.note: Seen spectroscopically and separated from erbia.

elementalForm.description: Holmium shares three valence electrons; it has the highest magnetic moment of any natural element.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Holmium has the strongest magnetic moment of any element and is used to concentrate fields in the most powerful magnets.
uses: Pole pieces for very strong magnets
facts: Holmium oxide glass is a standard for checking spectrometers.

discovery.note: Separated from yttria along with terbium.

elementalForm.description: Erbium shares three valence electrons in a hexagonal metallic lattice.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Silvery metal; its salts are pink.
summary: Erbium ions amplify light at 1,550 nm, the wavelength that carries internet signals through optical fibers across oceans.
uses: Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers for the internet
facts: Without erbium amplifiers, transoceanic fiber-optic internet would need far more repeater stations.

nameOrigin: Thule, an ancient name for the far north.

elementalForm.description: Thulium shares three valence electrons in a hexagonal metallic lattice.

summary: Thulium is the second rarest lanthanide. Thulium-170 makes compact X-ray sources and its lasers are used in surgery.
facts: Thulium is rarer in the crust than silver or iodine.

elementalForm.description: Ytterbium keeps a full 4f14 shell and shares only two 6s electrons, so its metal is soft and less dense than its neighbors.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Ytterbium atoms power some of the most accurate optical atomic clocks. Ytterbium-doped fiber lasers cut and weld metal in industry.
uses: Fiber lasers for cutting and welding
facts: Ytterbium lattice clocks keep time to better than one part in 10^18.

discovery.by: Georges Urbain; Carl Auer von Welsbach; Charles James
discovery.note: Three chemists separated it from ytterbia independently.

nameOrigin: Lutetia, the Latin name of Paris.

radioactive.note: 2.599% of natural lutetium; used to date meteorites.
Used in targeted prostate and neuroendocrine cancer therapy.

elementalForm.description: Lutetium (4f14 5d1 6s2) shares three valence electrons; the lanthanide contraction makes it the densest and hardest lanthanide.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Lutetium is the last lanthanide. Lutetium-177 is used in modern targeted radiotherapy for prostate cancer.
facts: A 2021 IUPAC project report recommends placing lutetium, not lanthanum, below yttrium in group 3.
